abstract: Accurately reconstructing networks of biochemical reactions is a crucial yet unsolved problem for leveraging advances in experimental techniques that track intracellular dynamics in a time-resolved fashion. This task is further challenged by the fact that we typically observe only part of the system, while many variables shaping the dynamics remain unobserved. Causal discovery methods can infer causal relations from purely observational data and account for unobserved variables. They therefore hold promise for yielding faithful, mechanistically interpretable representations of underlying biochemical interactions, but their potential in this context remains underexplored. In this work, we provide a systematic benchmark of state-of-the-art temporal causal discovery methods (tMIIC, PCMCI+/LPCMCI and SVAR-FCI) on time-series data from simulations of biochemical kinetics of mass action and Michaelis-Menten type modelled as systems of nonlinear stochastic differential equations, including an experimentally calibrated model of the epidermal growth factor receptor signalling network. By selectively omitting data, we consider the problem of reconstructing these networks in the presence of both latent confounders and unobserved species participating in reactions. We find that tMIIC and PCMCI+/LPCMCI achieve the highest overall prediction quality, with tMIIC able to handle larger samples within the same runtime budget. We identify, as the main condition for optimal performance of causal discovery, the consistency between data-sampling regimes (sampling intervals, trajectory length) and the typical timescales of the system. We establish that causal discovery can detect latent confounders via bidirected edges and unobserved species via time-delayed edges, locating hidden effects and encoding information on their typical timescales, provided that the data sampling guarantees adequate temporal resolution. As such, our results can guide the choice of hyperparameters in causal discovery algorithms and of data-sampling regimes to optimize network-reconstruction performance.
